t: The Scythians were Iranian-speaking horse nomads who from the 7th century BCE dominated the steppe north of the Black Sea, campaigned across the Near East and defied Darius I of Persia.
They left no writing of their own: we know them from Greek writers, above all Herodotus, who gave them most of Book 4 of his Histories, and from thousands of excavated burial mounds.
Their gold work of stags, panthers and griffins, and the treasures Greek goldsmiths made for their kings, belong to a wider Scythian world of related cultures that reached the Altai and Mongolia.
dyk: Herodotus says the Scythians sent the invading Darius I a bird, a mouse, a frog and five arrows; one Persian read it as a warning that unless they could fly, burrow or swim away, Scythian arrows would kill them all.
ev: The kurgan of Arzhan 1 is raised in Tuva, the earliest known burial with Scythian weapons, harness and animal art
Assyrian texts name the Scythians and their king Bartatua, who asks Esarhaddon for an Assyrian princess in marriage
By Herodotus’s account, the Scythians of Madyes rule “Asia” for 28 years and raid as far as Palestine
Darius I crosses the Danube to invade Scythia and withdraws without forcing a battle
Royal kurgans such as Solokha, Chertomlyk and Tovsta Mohyla are raised on the lower Dnieper
King Ateas, who had extended his rule to the Danube, is killed fighting Philip II of Macedon
Diophantus, general of Mithridates VI, defeats the Crimean Scythians of King Palakus
Scythian Neapolis in Crimea is destroyed, probably by the Goths, ending the Late Scythian kingdom

f.homeland: The steppe and forest-steppe north of the Black Sea, in present-day Ukraine, southern Russia and Crimea; related peoples of a wider “Scythian world” lived east across Kazakhstan to the Altai, Tuva and Mongolia
f.period: Scythian-type burials from c. 800 BCE in Tuva; the Scythians of the Black Sea steppe from the 7th century BCE, at their height in the 4th; a Late Scythian kingdom in Crimea until the 3rd century CE
f.known: Mounted archery; gold in the animal style; royal burial mounds such as Chertomlyk, Solokha and Tovsta Mohyla; the frozen tombs of Pazyryk; the failure of Darius I’s invasion
f.sources: Herodotus’s Histories, above all Book 4; Assyrian and Persian texts; the Hippocratic Airs, Waters, Places; excavated burial mounds and settlements from the Danube to Tuva; Greek-made gold showing Scythians; ancient DNA
